questions.stem: `emails` holds n different addresses. How does the running time of `first_repeat` grow as n grows?

options.why: One visible loop, but `in` on a list is a hidden loop over `seen`.
`in` on a list doesn't search by halves; lists aren't kept sorted.
options.origin: misconception: lists are searched like sorted arrays

options.why: It returns early only when it finds a repeat. With n different addresses it never does, so it checks everything.
options.origin: misconception: best case taken for worst case

questions.explain: The loop runs n times, and `e in seen` on line 5 checks the list `seen` item by item. `seen` grows by one each pass, so the checks add up to 0 + 1 + … + (n − 1) = n(n − 1)/2 comparisons: Θ(n²). (Θ is a tight bound: it grows in proportion to n², no faster and no slower.)

static: `e in seen` checks the list `seen` item by item
the loop on line 4 runs once per item of `emails`

questions.stem: A reviewer suggests changing line 3 to `seen = set()` and line 7 to `seen.add(e)`. What would change when `emails` is long?

options.text: It gets faster, but it can return a different email, because sets have no order
options.why: The order that matters here is the loop's order over `emails`, which doesn't change. `seen` is only asked yes/no questions.
options.origin: misconception: set order leaks into the result

options.text: Same results, and the running time becomes Θ(n) on average instead of Θ(n²)
Nothing: `in` checks a set item by item, just like a list
options.why: Sets are hash tables: `in` jumps to where the item would be instead of scanning.

options.text: It gets slower, because hashing an email costs more than comparing two emails
options.why: Hashing costs a little per lookup, but it replaces a scan of the whole list. Measured, the set version was faster at every size tried, from 1,000 to 8,000 emails.
options.origin: misconception: constant cost mistaken for growth

questions.explain: Checking membership in a set is a hash lookup, O(1) on average, so the loop does a constant amount of work per email. The function still returns the first repeat, because the loop order is unchanged. ("On average": many hash collisions could make lookups slower.)
